Hold two clock faces side by side: you can read the elapsed time between them without caring what hour either shows. The head that wishes to attend “exactly one step back” now needs to learn just one thing — the fixed angular signature of *adjacency* — and that single lesson is valid at position ten and position ten thousand alike. Relative structure, learned once, applied everywhere. That, mechanically, is how the previous-token head of our first episode knows its business.

Two footnotes, and the second touches your bench, sir. The first: notice that the rotation is applied to queries and keys *only* — the values pass untouched. Position, in this scheme, influences *where* a head looks and leaves no stamp on *what* it carries. The architecture has quietly filed position with the routing department rather than the cargo department — and you will see in a moment, when we come to the seam, that this is exactly the department where one would wish it filed.

The second footnote is the practical dividend. Because position lives in those rotation speeds, it can be *renegotiated after training*. A model trained on contexts of a certain length, asked to serve far longer ones, meets rotation angles it has never seen — the hands of the clock in positions no training example ever produced. But slow the hands — rescale the rotation speeds so that the old, familiar range of angles is stretched to cover the new length — and the model finds the geometry recognisable again. This trick, in its several refinements, is how practitioners have repeatedly stretched context windows well past their training lengths with only modest fine-tuning, and it is a pleasing early instance of the bargain this course keeps advertising: understand the mechanism, and the mechanism becomes adjustable. There are rival schemes — one simply taxes attention scores in proportion to distance, which has a certain fiscal directness — but rotation is the incumbent, and the incumbent is well dug in.

The hole is patched. The clerk knows the order of the pages. Now we may step back and look at the seam.

### Part Four — The Seam: One Head, Two Machines

Here is the observation that founded the modern science of transformer circuits, and it is, once you have the mechanism in hand, almost embarrassingly simple. I shall state it and then earn it.

The observation: the *attention pattern* — the decision of *where* to look — and the *content moved* — the decision of *what* to write — are computed by *entirely separate parts* of the head, from *entirely separate* sets of parameters, and *neither depends on the other*. The head, which presents itself as a single integrated operation, in fact factors cleanly into two independent circuits. The field gives them rather ungainly names, and to spare the synthesiser I shall translate. The first I shall call the **query-key circuit** — the *where-to-look* machine. The second I shall call the **output-value circuit** — the *what-to-write* machine.

Let me earn the claim by tracing the dependencies, which we have already laid out and need only collect. The attention pattern came from queries and keys. The queries and keys came, by their two lenses, from the notebook entries. So the where-to-look machine is: *read the notebook, decide which positions should attend to which*. It produces a pattern of weights. It touches the *values* not at all; it does not know or care what content lives at any position. It is concerned purely with *relevance* — with the geometry of questions and advertisements.

The content moved came from values and the output projection. The values came, by their lens, from the notebook entries. So the what-to-write machine is: *given that the present position attends to some earlier position, take that position’s content, transform it, and write it here*. It produces the actual deposit into the notebook. And it touches the *queries and keys* not at all; it does not decide *where* to look. Hand it an attention pattern from outside, and it will faithfully move content according to that pattern, indifferent to how the pattern was chosen.

So the two machines are genuinely decoupled. The where-to-look machine settles the routing; the what-to-write machine settles the cargo. You could, in principle, take the routing from one head and the cargo-handling from another and bolt them together, and each piece would do its job without complaint. *Where* and *what* are orthogonal questions, answered by orthogonal hardware.

I shall add one refinement for the connoisseur, because it sharpens the picture and it changed how the field does its sums. Notice that the query lens and the key lens never act separately — every use to which either is ever put is the comparison of one against the other. The mathematics duly obliges: the two lenses collapse into a *single* combined object, one transformation that takes a pair of notebook entries and returns a relevance score directly. And likewise on the other side of the seam: the value lens and the output projection collapse into a single transformation that takes an attended entry and returns the deposit to be written. The four lenses, in other words, pair off into two products — and only the products are real. You could alter the query lens however you pleased, compensate precisely in the key lens, and the head’s behaviour would not change by a hair; so there is no fact of the matter about what a query “really is” apart from the keys it is destined to meet. It is rather like a lock and its key, sir: the cutting of either, taken alone, is an arbitrary convention; the engineering fact is the fit. When the field analyses a head, accordingly, it analyses the two combined machines — never the four lenses separately, which would be studying the bookkeeping rather than the books.

Now, why does this decomposition matter so enormously for interpretability? Two reasons, and the second is subtle and important.

The first reason is simply that it *halves the problem*. To understand a head, you no longer face one tangled object; you face two simpler ones, and you can interrogate each on its own. You can ask of the where-to-look machine: *under what circumstances does this head attend from one position to another?* — and answer it by studying that machine in isolation. And you can ask of the what-to-write machine: *given that it attends somewhere, what does it copy, and how does it transform it?* — and answer that in isolation too. Two clean questions instead of one muddy one.

The second reason concerns *where in the notebook each machine reads and writes*, and it returns us to a theme from the first episode. Recall that the residual stream has twelve thousand dimensions, but that the queries, keys, and values are *much smaller* — a hundred or so dimensions, typically. This is forced by the arithmetic: the lenses that produce queries, keys, and values are transformations that *compress* the twelve-thousand-dimensional notebook entry down into a few-hundred-dimensional query or key or value. They are, in the mathematician’s term, *low-rank* — they can only see, and only express, a small subspace of the full stream.

The consequence is lovely and worth dwelling on. Because the where-to-look machine reads through these compressing lenses, it does *not* see the whole notebook entry when it decides where to attend. It sees only a small *slice* of it — a few hundred directions out of twelve thousand. It is, in effect, reading only a particular *column* of the notebook to make its routing decision, blind to the rest. Likewise the what-to-write machine reads only a particular slice of the attended position’s entry, and writes only into a particular slice of the present position’s entry. Each head, in other words, *reads from a few directions of the residual stream and writes to a few directions of it* — and is otherwise entirely uninvolved with the vast remainder.

This is the deep reason that *many heads can share one notebook without trampling each other*. Each head has staked out its own small subspace to read from and its own small subspace to write to. They are like a great many clerks all annotating the same enormous ledger, but each confined to his own narrow column — one minding the dates, another the sums, another the marginal cross-references — so that all may work the same page at once without collision. We met, last episode, the idea that *concepts* share the residual stream by pointing in nearly-perpendicular directions. Here is its operational cousin: *heads* share the residual stream by reading and writing in nearly-separate subspaces. The notebook is roomy, and everyone has agreed, more or less, to keep to his own column.

### Part Five — Many Heads, and the Curious Fact of No Privileged Direction

I have been speaking of *a* head, in the singular, but of course a real model has a great many. A large model may have something like a hundred heads at each of its ninety-odd layers — many thousands of heads in all. Let me say briefly how they coexist, because it sharpens the picture and because it sets up a point I shall need in two episodes’ time.

Within a single layer, the heads operate *in parallel and independently*. Each has its own three lenses — its own way of forming queries, keys, and values — and therefore its own where-to-look machine and its own what-to-write machine. Each surveys the text, makes its own routing decision, gathers its own cargo, and writes its own contribution into the notebook. And then — exactly as the first episode’s additive principle demands — *all their contributions are summed* into the residual stream. The layer’s total effect on the notebook is just the sum of what its many heads each independently decided to add. No head consults another within the layer; they are simultaneous and separate, and the stream simply collects them all.

This means that different heads, even in the very same layer, can be doing utterly different jobs — and, as we shall see in a moment, they do, with a specialisation that would gratify a guild.

But first, the point I promised, which concerns the *geometry* of the notebook and which I raised in passing last time. I claimed, last episode, that the model stores concepts as *directions*, and that these directions need not, and generally do not, line up with the coordinate axes — with the individual numbers in the list. I asked you to take that partly on faith, the Othello board notwithstanding. I can now give you the structural reason, and it is a small jewel of an argument.

The residual stream has what is called *no privileged basis*. Let me unpack the phrase. A “basis” is a choice of axes — a set of directions you decide to call the coordinate directions, against which everything else is measured. To say a space has *no privileged basis* is to say that *no particular choice of axes is special* — that you could rotate the entire coordinate system to any orientation you liked, and *nothing about the model’s behaviour would change*. The reason this holds for the residual stream is precisely the low-rank lenses we just discussed. Every head reads the stream only through its query, key, and value transformations, and writes to it only through its output projection. If you were to rotate the coordinates of the stream, you could *equally* rotate all those transformations to match, and the products — the actual numbers the model computes — would be identical. The rotation washes out. In the architecture as drawn on the blackboard, the model cannot tell, and does not care, which way the axes point.

And here is the consequence that justifies last episode’s claim. If no orientation of the axes is special, then *there is no reason for a concept to align itself with any particular axis*. A concept — the “French” direction, say — is free to point any which way, at any angle to the coordinate directions, because the coordinate directions are themselves arbitrary. So features are *directions*, full stop, and reading a feature off a single coordinate — the naive one-number-per-idea theory we demolished last time — is hopeless not by accident but by the deep symmetry of the architecture. The notebook has no preferred handwriting direction; the clerks write at whatever slant they please.

One honest asterisk, sir, before we bank the doctrine — and I give it to you because you of all listeners will collide with it at the bench. The beautiful symmetry is a property of the *idealised* architecture, and training does not entirely respect it. The normalisation layers between the blocks carry a small learned scale for each individual coordinate — parameters nailed to the axes — and the optimiser itself treats every coordinate separately when it updates the weights. Between them they leave fingerprints: trained models reliably develop a handful of *outlier dimensions*, individual coordinates of grotesquely outsized magnitude — the very rogue coordinates that make activation quantisation such a delicate business on your own bench. So state the doctrine with care. The architecture assigns the axes no *meaning*, and a concept has no reason whatever to align itself with them — that argument stands, and everything we built upon it stands. But the training process does leave the axes faintly marked, and the flat claim that nothing in a real residual stream knows where they point would be tidier than the truth. File the outlier dimensions where you keep the tuned lens: a reminder that the specimen on the bench is always a little less symmetrical than the one on the blackboard.

I flag, and set aside for Episode Four, that *one* part of the model is different — the interior of the feed-forward clerk, where a certain operation *does* break this symmetry and *does* single out the coordinate axes as special. That exception is the seed of a great deal of trouble, and it is the reason the word *neuron* still means something, faintly, in one corner of the model. But that is two episodes away. For now: the residual stream has no privileged direction, and therefore features point everywhere, and therefore we shall need cleverer instruments than “read off the numbers” to find them.

I did, however, promise you the specialisation of the heads, and it deserves better than a passing remark. The cataloguing of heads is one of the field’s oldest occupations, and the catalogue is worth an excursion of its own.

### Part Six — A Field Guide to Heads

When the interpretability researcher confronts a new model, one of the first orders of business is a census: go head by head, and determine what each one does. The seam tells us how to conduct it. For each head, interrogate the two machines separately — show the where-to-look machine a great variety of texts and observe where its attention lands; inspect the what-to-write machine to see what cargo it carries when it gets there. The work has the flavour of Victorian natural history — long days in the field, a notebook of one’s own, the gradual emergence of species — and like Victorian natural history it has produced a recognisable fauna. A surprising number of heads turn out to have crisp, nameable jobs, and the same species recur, model after model, with the regularity that the first episode taught us to call universality. Let me give you the principal specimens.

The **previous-token head** you have already met: it attends, from every position, exactly one step back, and carries forward a summary of what it finds there. The rotary clock is what makes its trick mechanically possible; the induction circuit is what makes it famous. There are cousins at other fixed offsets, and heads that attend preferentially to the beginning of the current sentence or clause — the *positional* family generally, navigating by the clock more than by content.

The **duplicate-token head** is the natural-born detective of the family: it attends, from a token, back to earlier occurrences of *the very same token*. Its where-to-look machine asks, in effect, “where have I appeared before?” — the query naming the token’s own identity, the keys answering in kind. When a name like Fink-Nottle turns up a second time in a passage, it is a duplicate-token head that first registers the recurrence — a name of that sort, once encountered, not being readily mistaken for another. Remember this specimen; it will testify at length in our sixth episode.

The **successor head** is a more startling find. It attends to a token that belongs to some conventional ordered sequence — a day of the week, a month, a numeral, a letter of the alphabet — and what its what-to-write machine deposits is a push toward the *next* element of the sequence. Shown Monday, it promotes Tuesday; shown March, April; shown seven, eight. Monday is followed by Tuesday with a reliability one wishes attached to certain other engagements. The head amounts to a little learned *increment* operation — and the same specimen has been found across model families of quite different sizes and pedigrees, which is universality again: incrementation, it seems, is a tool every model decides it needs, and they all build it in recognisably the same place.

There are heads that attend from a pronoun back to candidate referents; heads that track quotation marks, attending to where the current quotation opened; heads that mind the subject of the sentence across its interruptions. There are the **negative heads** I mentioned in our first episode — the objectors — whose cargo *opposes* a prediction that other components are promoting; the best-studied of them attend to a token that has appeared before and write, precisely, a vote *against* repeating it, a learned check on the model’s own enthusiasm for parroting itself. And there are the **name-mover heads**, which fetch a person’s name from earlier in a passage and deposit it at the point of prediction — the star witnesses of the sixth episode’s courtroom drama, where we shall watch them, their backups, and their saboteurs all at work in a single traced circuit.

And then there is the institution I promised in Part Two. Survey real attention patterns at scale and you find something that looks, at first, like an epidemic of idleness: head after head spending the bulk of its attention, on the bulk of tokens, on the *very first position* in the text — a position that frequently holds nothing more nutritious than a ceremonial beginning-of-text marker. Naive inspection concludes that the model is fascinated by its own first word. The truth is our old friend the fixed budget. A head whose trigger is absent — the duplicate-token head in a passage with no duplicates, the quotation head in a passage with no quotations — *must spend its unit of attention somewhere*, and the model has learned to designate the first position as the place where unwanted attention is dumped: a wastepaper basket, institutionalised. The field calls it the **attention sink**. The head is not studying the first token; it is declining, in the only grammar available to it, to study anything. Many heads thus spend most of their existence dormant at the sink, springing to life only when their particular quarry appears in the text — a pattern less like an office of busy clerks than like a fire brigade: idle, by design, nearly always.

The catalogue should also come with a warning label, and I would be failing in my duties if I did not affix it. Attention patterns are the most *photogenic* objects in this entire science — bright heat-maps showing which words look at which — and they have accordingly become the most popular, and the most carelessly read. The temptation is to treat the pattern as the explanation: the model attended from here to there, and therefore *that* is why it did what it did. But you now know the seam, and the seam says otherwise. Attention is only the routing; whether the routing *matters* depends entirely on the cargo, and the cargo is the other machine’s department. A head may attend strongly to a position while its what-to-write machine carries essentially nothing of consequence from it — the clerk may stare at a page for minutes, sir, and write nothing; the staring is data, not verdict. And the sink makes matters worse, since the single largest destination of attention in the whole model is, by construction, meaningless. The corrective discipline is always the same: never read the where-machine without auditing the what-machine. Much of the early literature’s enthusiasm for attention maps as explanations did not survive this audit, and the field’s standards are the better for the funeral.

### Part Seven — The Engineer’s Dividend: An Archive of Keys and Values

I promised in the first episode that understanding mechanisms pays engineering dividends, and attention supplies the clearest cases on record — several of which are sitting, at this moment, in your serving stack, sir. Permit me a brief excursion to the machine room. It will cost us nothing; the mechanism we have built this hour is exactly the mechanism that runs the bill.

Consider what happens when a model *generates*, one token at a time. To produce the next token, the newest position must form its queries and compare them against the keys of *every* position before it, then gather the corresponding values. But here is the saving grace, and it follows from causal masking: the keys and values of the *past* positions never change. A past position attends only backward; nothing the future does can revise its notebook entry, and so its keys and its values, once computed, are final. It would be madness to recompute them for every new token — and so nobody does. They are computed once and *archived*: every position’s keys and values, for every head, at every layer, held in memory for the rest of the conversation. The field calls this archive the **key-value cache**, and the act of generation is thereby reduced, at each step, to one new query interrogating a great stored library of old advertisements and old goods.

Now do the bookkeeping, because the bookkeeping is where the economics of your profession lives. The archive grows with every token: per token, per layer, per head, a key and a value. For a large model this comes to a meaningful fraction of a megabyte for every single token of context — multiply by a context of a hundred thousand tokens and the archive for *one conversation* runs to tens of gigabytes, a warehouse beginning to rival the model’s own weights. The celebrated cost of long contexts is, at bottom, the cost of warehousing advertisements and goods; and the speed of generation is governed less by arithmetic than by how fast that warehouse can be read. When you size a batch, sir, you are, whether the dashboard says so or not, allocating shelving.

Once the structure is seen, the optimisations almost propose themselves — and each is an interpretability observation wearing overalls. The first: notice that the *diversity* a layer needs lives mostly in its questions. Many heads asking many different questions is the whole point of multi-headed attention; but must every head also keep its *own* shelf of advertisements and goods? The field’s answer was no: let *groups* of query-heads share a single set of keys and values among them. This is **grouped-query attention**, standard in the current generation of open-weights models, and it shrinks the archive several-fold — commonly eight-fold — at modest cost in quality; the extreme version, every query-head in a layer sharing one communal shelf, goes by *multi-query attention*. For the cataloguer of heads there is small print worth reading: in such models the where-to-look machines remain individual, but the cargo is communal — the heads in a group may ask different questions, yet whatever position they attend to, they draw from the same shelf of goods — each retaining only its own way of formatting the shared cargo for deposit. The seam, you notice, is what makes the bargain even thinkable: routing and cargo are separate machines, so one may be economised without touching the other.

The second optimisation is my favourite, because its pedigree is pure interpretability. Recall the attention sink — the wastepaper basket at position one. When a conversation outruns the archive and something must be evicted, the obvious policy is to discard the *oldest* tokens first. Try it naively and the model degrades — not gracefully, but precipitously, into incoherence. The diagnosis comes straight from the census: you have thrown away the sink. Thousands of dormant heads, obliged by the softmax to spend their budget somewhere, have lost the somewhere — and their obligatory attention, denied its basket, smears across the remaining positions as noise in every layer at once. The remedy, once the mechanism is understood, is almost comically cheap: when evicting, *always keep the first few tokens*, forever, alongside a sliding window of recent ones, and discard from the middle. Do that, and models stream coherently over millions of tokens. The fix arrived in the very paper that named the sink — diagnosis and remedy published in one stroke — and it is the cleanest specimen I can offer you of this course’s standing bargain: a mechanism read is a mechanism exploited. And the bargain has since closed its loop at the factory itself: the newest generation of open models ships with the basket *designed in* — a dedicated sink token, or a small learned escape valve in each head’s softmax — the institution the field discovered by census now installed by the architects on purpose. The seam, meanwhile, has yielded a third exploitation: DeepSeek’s *latent attention*, which compresses the shelf itself — keys and values held as a single shared low-rank latent, unpacked only at the moment of use — shrinking the warehouse not by sharing shelves but by folding them. And the newest open models of the Gemma class economise along the other axis entirely, interleaving layers that attend only to a recent sliding window with the occasional full-span layer, so that most of the archive is simply never kept. The remainder of the menagerie — the quantising of the archive, the paging of it as an operating system pages memory — I leave to your professional literature, which I believe keeps you adequately supplied.

The excursion is over; back to the science. We have heads in the singular, and a census of their species. What we do not yet have is the thing that makes them an *intelligence* rather than a guild of savants: cooperation.

### Part Eight — Composition: How Heads in Different Layers Conspire

Everything so far has concerned heads acting *alone*. But the real power — and the source of every interesting circuit in this science — comes from heads *cooperating across layers*. And the mechanism of their cooperation follows directly from the additive notebook, so directly that you could almost derive it yourself.

Here is the situation. A head in an early layer reads the notebook, does its work, and *adds its contribution* to the stream. That contribution now sits in the notebook. The stream flows upward. A head in a *later* layer then reads the notebook — and what it reads *includes the earlier head’s contribution*, because nothing erased it. So the later head’s queries, keys, and values are computed from a notebook entry that *the earlier head helped to write*. The later head is, in effect, *reading the earlier head’s output as part of its input*. This is called **composition**, and it is how isolated heads become multi-step algorithms.

Now recall that the later head has three lenses — query, key, value — and the earlier head’s contribution can flow into *any* of them. This gives three distinct flavours of composition, and the distinctions matter, because different circuits use different flavours.

The first flavour I shall call **query composition**. Here, the earlier head writes something into the notebook that the later head reads *through its query lens* — so the earlier head influences *what the later head is looking for*. The earlier head, you might say, *poses the later head’s question*. It reaches forward and adjusts the query, changing the target of the later head’s search.

The second flavour I shall call **key composition**. Here, the earlier head writes something that the later head reads *through its key lens* — so the earlier head influences *which positions advertise themselves* to the later head. The earlier head is *relabelling the filing system*, changing the advertisements that the later head’s query will be compared against. This one is subtle, and it is the heart of the most famous circuit in the field, so hold it with particular care: an early head can write, at some position, a note that *changes how that position advertises itself* to a head in the layer above.

The third flavour I shall call **value composition**. Here, the earlier head’s contribution flows into the later head’s *value lens* — so it changes *what content the later head will carry* when it attends to that position. The earlier head is *altering the goods on the shelf*, so that when the later head retrieves from that position, it retrieves something the earlier head placed there.

Where to look — through queries and keys — and what to carry — through values. Composition can reach into any of the three. And when it does, the two heads together compute something *neither could compute alone*. The field sometimes speaks, evocatively, of *virtual heads* — the idea that a pair of composed heads behaves like a single, more sophisticated head that does not physically exist anywhere in the model but emerges from the collaboration. Two clerks, each simple, who by leaving notes for one another in the shared ledger accomplish jointly a task that would baffle either singly.

I want you to feel the *shape* of what composition buys, even before we see a specific instance next episode, because it is the whole reason depth matters. A single head can only attend based on what is *directly written* at each position — the raw content of the notebook as it stands. But a *composed* pair can attend based on something *computed* — because the early head can first write a *derived* fact into the notebook, and the later head can then attend based on *that*. Depth, in other words, lets the model attend not merely to *what is there* but to *what it has worked out*. The notebook is not only read; it is *progressively annotated*, and later clerks may act on the annotations of earlier ones. That progressive annotation is the source of nearly everything sophisticated a transformer does.

### Part Nine — The Ladder: What One Layer Can and Cannot Do

To make the value of composition concrete — to show you that depth is not a luxury but a hard necessity for certain computations — let me walk up a little ladder of toy models, each one layer taller than the last. This is a classic pedagogical device in the field, and it is illuminating precisely because at each rung we can say *exactly* what the model can and cannot express.

The bottom rung: a model with **zero attention layers**. Strip out attention entirely. Such a model can do nothing but map the current token, in isolation, to a guess about the next one — because with no attention, no information crosses between positions, and each position sees only itself. What it learns is therefore a *bigram* table: for each possible current word, the marginal likelihood of each possible next word. “The word ‘the’ is often followed by a noun.” A lookup table of pairs, and nothing more. It has no notion of context whatever; the words before the current one might as well not exist. A creature of pure local reflex.

The next rung: a model with **one attention layer**. Now information can cross between positions — once. A single head can attend from the present position back to *one* earlier position and bring something forward. What can such a model express? It can learn what are called *skip-trigrams* — patterns of the form “if a certain word appeared *somewhere* earlier, and the current word is such-and-such, then predict so-and-so.” The where-to-look machine selects which earlier word to attend to; the what-to-write machine copies or transforms it into a prediction. This is a real gain over bigrams: the model can now let a distant word influence the present guess. If the word “open” appeared earlier, the present word “the” might be steered toward “door.”

But here is the instructive part — the *defect* of the one-layer model, which exposes exactly what a single attention step cannot do. Because the where-to-look machine and the what-to-write machine are *decoupled*, and because each sees only its own endpoints, a single head can attend to an earlier word and copy *something about that word* — but it cannot *condition what it copies on a second word*. It can say “having attended to ‘open’, predict ‘door’.” What it cannot cleanly say is “having attended to ‘open’, predict whatever word *followed* ‘open’ last time” — because to do *that*, it would need to first know what followed ‘open’, which is a fact about a *different* position, a fact that no single attention step has had the chance to compute and write down. The one-layer head is stuck attending on the basis of *raw tokens* and copying on the basis of *raw tokens*. It cannot attend on the basis of a *relationship between tokens*, because computing that relationship would itself require an attention step, and it has spent its only one.

This shows up as a characteristic class of errors — the field calls them *skip-trigram bugs* — where the one-layer model, having learned “attend to a quotation mark and expect another quotation mark,” cannot distinguish *which* quotation mark should match *which*, and produces confidently wrong completions. The bug is not a failure of training; it is a *mathematical limit* of one attention layer. The head simply lacks the expressive power to represent the conditional structure, and no amount of training will conjure it.

The next rung: a model with **two attention layers**. And now, with composition newly possible, the limit lifts. The first layer’s head can compute a *relationship* — for instance, “the word at this position was preceded by such-and-such” — and *write that relationship into the notebook*. The second layer’s head can then attend on the basis of that *written-down relationship*, by key composition, doing what the one-layer model provably could not: attend not to a raw token but to a token *characterised by its context*. And the first useful thing this newfound power produces is precisely the operation the one-layer model failed at — “find where the current pattern occurred before, and predict whatever followed it then.” That operation has a name. It is the **induction head**. And it is the entire subject of our next episode.

I want the moral of the ladder to land cleanly, because it justifies the architecture of everything to come. The jump from one attention layer to two is not a quantitative jump — a bit more of the same. It is a *qualitative* one. One layer can *copy a token it has seen*. Two layers can *look a token up by its context*. That is the difference between a clerk who can fetch a page you point to and a clerk who can fetch the page that *follows* the page matching a description you give him — between retrieval and *associative* retrieval. And the whole leap is purchased by *composition*: by one head writing a note that another head acts upon. Depth, in a transformer, is the depth of *annotation* — the number of times the notebook can be marked up before a later clerk must read it and decide. Each additional layer is one more round of “work something out, write it down, and let the next clerk build on it.” That is what we buy when we stack.

### Closing — What We Have Earned, and Where It Points

Let us gather the episode.

Attention is the *one* mechanism by which information moves between positions in the text — the feed-forward clerks are sealed in their rooms, and so every act of relating one part of a passage to another must route through an attention head. That alone makes attention the natural home of the field’s circuits, because a circuit is, at bottom, a pattern of *movement*.

A single head works by three lenses upon each notebook entry — the **query**, the question; the **key**, the advertisement; the **value**, the goods. It compares queries against keys to decide *where to look*, apportioning a single fixed unit of attention by the softmax; and it gathers *values* according to that verdict to decide *what to write*, adding the result into the shared notebook. Position enters the comparison by the **rotary** trick — queries and keys turned like the hands of a many-speed clock, so that what the dot product sees is *relative* offset, the same lesson valid anywhere in the document, and renegotiable, conveniently, after training.

And the master discovery — the seam down which the head splits — is that *where to look* and *what to write* are computed by two **independent** machines: the **query-key circuit**, concerned only with relevance and routing, and the **output-value circuit**, concerned only with cargo. Decoupled — indeed, each a single combined object, a lock-and-key fit in which only the pairing is real — and therefore separately legible. Each, moreover, reads and writes only a small *subspace* of the twelve-thousand-dimensional notebook — which is how thousands of heads share one stream without collision, and which, together with the stream’s lack of any privileged direction, is why features are *directions* free to point anywhere.

The census conducted along that seam yields a recurring fauna — previous-token heads, duplicate-token heads, successor heads incrementing their way through the days of the week, negative heads voting against the model’s own enthusiasms, name-movers awaiting their trial in Episode Six — together with the **attention sink**, the institutional wastepaper basket where dormant heads park their obligatory budget; and with the standing caution that an attention pattern is routing, not explanation, until the cargo has been audited. The same mechanics, read with an engineer’s eye, run the economics of serving: the **key-value cache**, the archive whose shelving you allocate whenever you size a batch; grouped-query attention, which economises the goods while preserving the questions; and the sink-aware eviction that lets a model stream forever — mechanism read, mechanism exploited.

Finally, heads cooperate across layers by **composition** — an early head writing a note that a later head reads through its query, its key, or its value. Composition is what turns isolated heads into multi-step algorithms; it is the reason depth matters; and its first and most celebrated fruit is the *induction head*, the operation that a single attention layer provably cannot perform and that two layers can.

We have, in short, traded the airy notebook for its actual machinery. We know now, mechanically, who writes in the notebook, how they decide where to read, what they carry, what it costs to warehouse their goods — and we have found the one structural fact, *where* and *what* are separable, that lets a human being read an attention circuit at all.

In our next episode, we cash in the ladder’s promise. We shall take the induction head — which the first episode showed you as a conjuring trick and which this episode showed you to be *possible* only with two layers and composition — and we shall trace it to its last wire. And then I shall show you something that genuinely startled the people who discovered it: that a model’s ability to *learn within a single prompt*, with no change to its weights at all, does not develop gradually during training. It switches on, almost all at once, in a single sharp moment — and that moment is the moment these very heads are born. I shall have it ready.

Until then, sir.

*— End of Episode Two.*

## Episode 3 — Induction Heads and the Origin of In-Context Learning

*A Course in Mechanistic Interpretability — Episode Three*

### A Promise, and a Surprise

Good day, sir.

We arrive at the episode I have been looking forward to, because it is the one where the abstractions of the first two episodes pay a concrete and rather startling dividend. Permit me to remind you what we have already established.

From the first episode, you have the induction head itself — the circuit by which a model, shown a passage in which some name was followed by some second name, will, on meeting that first name again, confidently produce the second. I sketched its mechanism there: the previous-token head writing its annotation, the induction head matching on it. From the second episode, you have the *grammar* that makes such a thing possible — the three lenses, the seam between *where to look* and *what to write*, and above all **composition**, the business of one head writing a note into the shared notebook that a later head then reads and acts upon. I argued, by walking up a ladder of toy models, that this particular circuit is impossible for a model with a single attention layer and becomes possible with two.

What I gave you in the first episode was the working sketch — true, but quick, the version one draws on the back of an envelope. Today I make it rigorous: I shall trace the induction head to its last wire — exactly which two heads conspire, exactly what each writes and reads, exactly why two layers and not one, and exactly which flavour of composition does the work — so that the back-of-the-envelope version becomes a thing you could, in principle, build. That is the first portion of the episode, and it is satisfying in the way a well-made clock is satisfying.

But the later portions are where I must ask you to brace yourself slightly, because they contain one of the genuinely surprising empirical findings in this young science — the kind of finding that, when researchers first saw it, made them sit up. It concerns the moment in a model’s *training* when this machinery comes into being. One might reasonably expect a capability to accrue gradually — the model getting a little better at pattern-completion with each passing hour of training, as a student improves at scales. That is not what happens. The ability appears *suddenly*, in a narrow window, announced by a visible kink in the training curve — and at that same moment, a much larger and more important capability switches on alongside it, as though the two were the same event seen from two angles. They very nearly are.

That larger capability is the one we call *in-context learning* — the model’s ability to learn from the contents of its prompt, within a single forward pass, with not one of its weights changed. It is the thing that makes a large language model *useful*, the thing that lets you teach it a task by example in the moment rather than by retraining it for a week. And the finding I shall lay before you is that a great deal of this seemingly miraculous capacity rests on the very humble mechanism we are about to dissect. The grandest trick in the repertoire and one of the plainest turn out to be, to a considerable degree, the same trick.

A claim of that size deserves to be earned rather than asserted, and the researchers who made it assembled the evidence with a thoroughness I intend to honour: not one argument but six, stacked from suggestive to surgical, and I shall give you all six. First, however, the clockwork.

### Part One — The Induction Head, Traced to Its Last Wire

I shall use the names we used in the first episode, for continuity and because they are agreeably absurd. We saw the mechanism sketched there; now we build it slowly enough to be sure of every joint. Suppose the model is reading a passage in which, some way back, the name **Honoria** was followed by the name **Glossop**. The text rolls on. And now, at the present position, the name **Honoria** appears *again*, and the model must guess what comes next. We — and the model, if it is any good — expect **Glossop**, because that is what followed Honoria the first time. The pattern, having occurred once, is expected to repeat.

I want to state the goal with care, because the whole mechanism is shaped to it. The model is at the second **Honoria**. It must somehow reach back, find the *earlier* place where Honoria occurred, look at *what came immediately after* it — Glossop — and bring *that* forward as its prediction. Notice the peculiar indirection. The model is not looking for Honoria; it already *is* at Honoria. It is looking for *the word that followed the previous Honoria*. It must attend not to a token but to a *position defined by its neighbour* — the position whose *predecessor* was Honoria. That indirection is precisely what a single attention layer cannot manage, and understanding *why* — not merely that two layers suffice, which you have, but why one cannot and two can — is the lesson.

Here is the machinery, in two heads across two layers.

**The first head, in an early layer, is a *previous-token head*.** Its job is humble and general: at every position, it attends to the position immediately before it — navigating, you now know, by the rotary clock or its positional kin — and copies some signature of that previous token into the present position’s notebook entry. It is one of those crisp, nameable heads from last episode’s field guide: its where-to-look machine does nothing cleverer than “attend one step back,” and its what-to-write machine copies a tag identifying the token it found there. So, in particular, at the position of the *first* **Glossop**, this head reaches back one step to **Honoria** and writes into Glossop’s entry a note that means, in the model’s private code, *“the token before me was Honoria.”* Glossop’s page in the notebook now carries, in addition to “I am Glossop,” the annotation “I was preceded by Honoria.” Mark that annotation. It is the linchpin.

**The second head, in a later layer, is the *induction head* proper.** It acts at the present position — the *second* **Honoria** — and it does something that is only possible because the previous-token head has already done its work. Recall from last episode the three flavours of composition, and recall that I asked you to hold *key composition* with particular care. Here is why.

The induction head forms its **query** from the present token. The present token is Honoria, and the induction head’s query lens is trained to convert “I am the token Honoria” into the question *“find me the position that was preceded by Honoria.”* That is the question it broadcasts. Now it compares this query, as every head does, against the **keys** at all earlier positions — and here is the crucial part: the keys it is comparing against are *not* the raw keys of the original tokens. They have been *modified by the previous-token head’s annotations*. The key at the first **Glossop** position no longer advertises merely “I am Glossop.” Because the previous-token head wrote “preceded by Honoria” into Glossop’s entry, and because the induction head reads its keys through a lens that picks up exactly that annotation, the key at Glossop now advertises *“I am a position that was preceded by Honoria.”*

And so the match is made. The induction head’s query — *seeking: preceded-by-Honoria* — aligns precisely with Glossop’s modified key — *offering: preceded-by-Honoria* — and the induction head attends, from the second Honoria, to the first Glossop. This is the *where to look* settled: the attention lands on exactly the position holding the word that followed Honoria last time. The field calls this behaviour **prefix matching** — the head matches the present context against the prefix of an earlier occurrence — and you will note that it is achieved entirely by the query-key circuit, the where-to-look machine, operating on annotations that an earlier head supplied. That is key composition in the flesh: the earlier head *relabelled the filing system*, and the later head’s query found the relabelled file.

The *what to write* is now almost anticlimactic, and it is handled by the induction head’s output-value circuit. Having attended to the Glossop position, the head copies Glossop’s identity forward — boosts, in the model’s final reckoning, the probability of the token Glossop. The field calls this second behaviour **copying**: having found the right position, faithfully reproduce what is there. And copying is just the output-value machine doing the plainest thing it can do — carry the cargo across unaltered.

So the induction head is, exactly, the marriage of two sub-abilities: **prefix matching** in the where-to-look machine — find the position whose past matches my present — and **copying** in the what-to-write machine — bring forward what you find there. Two simple competencies, in the two decoupled halves of one head, riding on an annotation laid down by a head one layer below. One honesty clause before the certificate is framed: the trace I have given is the classic construction, and it is not the only one nature uses — in some models the same behaviour is assembled along a different seam of composition, and real induction heads prove mechanically heterogeneous when examined closely. The one I traced is the canonical specimen, not the whole species.

Now I can discharge, rigorously, the debt from the ladder. *Why can one layer not do this?* Because the pivotal fact — “this position was preceded by Honoria” — is a *relationship between two positions*, and computing it requires an attention step: somebody must look back one token and write down what they saw. That is the previous-token head’s entire contribution, and it consumes one attention layer. Only *after* that fact is written into the notebook can a second head attend *on the basis of it*. A one-layer model has a single attention step; it must spend it either computing the relationship or using it, and it cannot do both. It is therefore stuck attending on the basis of *raw tokens* — which, as I showed you last time, yields the brittle skip-trigram and its characteristic bug. The induction head needs *two* steps because it needs to attend on the basis of something *previously computed*, and the only machinery for “previously computed and written down for later use” is depth. The induction head is the simplest interesting thing that genuinely requires the notebook to be marked up before it is read. It is, if you like, the *hello-world* of composition — the first program you can write that needs two clerks instead of one.

### Part Two — Measuring the Beast: The Telephone-Directory Test

Before we proceed to the surprise, a question of method, because it bears on everything after. I have described what an induction head does. How does one *find* them — how, confronting a model with thousands of heads, does one determine which are induction heads and which are not, without weeks of squinting at attention maps? The field’s answer is a diagnostic of such cunning simplicity that it deserves a minute of its own, and it will teach you something about experimental design in this science.

The trouble with testing pattern-completion on ordinary text is that ordinary text is full of alibis. Show the model “the cat sat on the” twice and watch it predict “mat” the second time, and you have proven nothing about induction — the model might predict “mat” from grammar, from semantics, from the sheer statistics of English, with no reference to the earlier occurrence at all. To isolate the mechanism, one must construct a text in which *every* alternative explanation has been removed — in which the *only* conceivable way to predict the next token is to consult the earlier repeat.

The construction: take a sequence of *completely random* tokens — words and word-fragments drawn from the vocabulary by lot, with no grammar, no meaning, no statistical regularity whatever — and then *repeat the sequence*, splicing a second copy directly after the first. The result is a passage with all the literary merit of a telephone directory read twice, which is precisely its virtue. In the first half, the model can predict nothing; every next token is a fresh roll of the dice, and the model’s loss on it is dismal, as it should be. But in the *second* half, every token is, in principle, perfectly predictable — *provided* the model can find the corresponding position in the first half and copy what follows it. No grammar will help; there is none. No world knowledge will help; the sequence means nothing. Prefix-match-and-copy is the only road to a correct answer, by construction.

This gives the field its two standard instruments, and you met their names in the mechanism. For any head, one measures a **prefix-matching score**: feed the repeated random sequence, and ask what fraction of the head’s attention, from each token in the second half, lands on the token *just after* that token’s earlier occurrence — the Glossop position, in our running example. And one measures a **copying score**: ask to what degree the head’s what-to-write machine, given what it finds there, actually promotes that token in the model’s output. A head scoring high on both is an induction head, certified — not by anecdote or by a suggestive heat-map, but by behaviour on a stimulus engineered to admit no other explanation. You will recognise the family resemblance to the synthetic curves of the first episode’s vision anatomists: when nature’s stimuli are ambiguous, manufacture unambiguous ones.

Run this census across models and a striking regularity appears: induction heads are *everywhere*. Every transformer language model of sufficient depth that anyone has examined contains them — small models, frontier models, models of different architectures and pedigrees, models trained by rival organisations on different data. Usually not one but a population of them, scattered across the middle layers. It is universality again, and in its strongest form yet: prefix-match-and-copy appears to be a solution so favoured by the task of language prediction that gradient descent finds it *every single time*. When a mechanism is rediscovered by every model that has ever been trained, one begins to suspect it is load-bearing. The next two parts are the demonstration of just how load-bearing.

### Part Three — The Bump: A Capability That Arrives All at Once

Now the surprise I promised, and it concerns *training* — the long process by which a model’s weights are gradually adjusted, over billions of examples, to predict text better and better.

One pictures this process as smooth. The model’s error — its *loss*, the single number measuring how badly it predicts the next token, averaged over a great deal of text — starts high and is driven steadily down, hour by hour, as the weights improve. And in the large, that picture is correct: the loss curve is, for the most part, a smooth and unremarkable descent, the kind of diminishing-returns slope you would sketch with your eyes closed.

But when researchers looked closely at this descent — in a careful study from twenty twenty-two that trained a whole family of transformers, from one layer up to many, and watched their innards as they learned — they found that it is not *perfectly* smooth. Early in training, there is a brief, distinct interruption: a short window in which the loss drops *faster* than the surrounding trend — a small but unmistakable kink in what should be a featureless slope. Before the window, the curve is doing one thing; after it, the curve is doing another; and across the window, something *changes*. The field has come to call this feature the **induction bump**, and the reason for the name is the heart of the matter.

When the researchers asked what was happening *inside* the model across exactly that window — what changed in the machinery between the start of the bump and its end — the answer was clean and specific. *That is when the induction heads form.* Before the window, the model has no induction heads; the prefix-matching scores of all its heads sit at the floor. Across the window, the wiring assembles itself — the two heads find their roles, the composition between them clicks into place, and the prefix-matching scores of particular heads climb from nothing to high. After the window, the induction heads are present and functioning. The bump in the loss curve is the *signature*, visible from outside, of a specific mechanism crystallising inside.

The timing has a regularity worth reporting. Across the family of models in the study — different sizes, different depths — the window arrived at roughly the same *age*: somewhere between about two and a half and five billion tokens into training. Early days, by the standards of a training run that consumes trillions; the machinery is assembled in the model’s infancy and merely refined thereafter. There is something quietly comic in the predictability of it — rather as one can forecast, to within a term, when an undergraduate will discover Nietzsche — but the scientific point is serious: a *developmental milestone*, arriving on schedule, in every member of the family.

I want you to feel why this is remarkable and not merely tidy. We are accustomed, in machine learning, to capabilities that improve *continuously* — a little better with each step, no special moments. What the induction bump shows is a capability that arrives *discontinuously* — a qualitative reorganisation of the model’s internal machinery, compressed into a narrow window, with a *before* and an *after* that differ in kind and not merely in degree. The model does not get *gradually* better at pattern completion. It is, for a while, simply unable to do it; then, over a short span, the apparatus for doing it *assembles*; and thereafter it can. This is, to date, the cleanest and most thoroughly understood example in the field of what people loosely call an *emergent capability* — a behaviour that appears abruptly — pinned down not by hand-waving but by an identified mechanism whose formation you can watch and whose moment of formation coincides exactly with the behaviour’s onset. We shall return to the larger question of emergence before the episode is out, because the induction bump turns out to have relatives, and the family portrait is instructive. But first, the main event.

### Part Four — In-Context Learning, and the Six Lines of Evidence

Here is the main event. To reach it I must first say, with some care, what *in-context learning* is, because the phrase is used loosely and the precise version is what matters.

A language model has two utterly different ways of acquiring a capability, and they must not be confused. The first is *training* — the slow adjustment of the weights I just described, which happens once, in the laboratory, over weeks, and is then frozen. When you converse with a deployed model, its weights are fixed; nothing you say changes them. The second way is the one that operates *at the moment you use it*, with the weights frozen: the model adjusts its behaviour *in response to the contents of its prompt*. You show it three examples of a task in the prompt, and it performs the task on the fourth item — not because anything was retrained, but because the examples are *sitting there in the context*, and the model, reading them, conditions its next prediction upon them. This second mode — *improvement in performance that comes from information present in the context, with no change to the weights* — is **in-context learning**. It is “learning” only in the loose sense that the model behaves as though it has learned; mechanically, it is a single forward pass that happens to be very good at exploiting the patterns laid out in its input. It is the entire basis of what people call *few-shot prompting* — teach by example, in the moment.

Now, the study did not only locate the induction bump. It also measured, across training, a quantity it called the **in-context learning score** — and I shall give you the actual recipe, because it is clever and concrete. The idea is to ask: *how much better does the model predict a token late in a passage than a token early in the same passage?* A token near the start must be predicted with very little context to draw on. A token far in can be predicted with the whole preceding passage available — and a model capable of in-context learning should exploit that accumulation. So the researchers took, as their score, the difference between the model’s loss at the *five-hundredth* token of a passage and its loss at the *fiftieth* — how much the intervening four hundred and fifty tokens of context actually *bought*. A model that cannot learn from context predicts the five-hundredth token no better than the fiftieth; the score sits near zero. A model that learns from context well predicts the late token far better; the score is large. That gap, tracked through training, is the in-context learning score.

And here is the finding, stated as plainly as I can manage. *The in-context learning score jumps — sharply, in a narrow window — at exactly the moment of the induction bump.* The two are not merely correlated in some vague way; they coincide in time, step for step, in every model of the family. At the precise span of training during which the induction heads assemble, the model’s general ability to profit from its context *switches on*. Before: the model treats late tokens little better than early ones. After: it exploits context dramatically better, and the in-context learning score, once it leaps, scarcely changes for the remainder of training — the capability arrives in that window and arrives essentially complete.

The natural and irresistible hypothesis is that the first *causes* the second — that in-context learning, at least in large part, *is* the generalised operation of induction machinery. Now, a coincidence in time, however crisp, is a correlation, and the researchers knew it. What gives the paper its lasting authority is that it did not stop there. It assembled *six* distinct lines of argument, in ascending order of surgical directness, and the architecture of the case is worth laying out — two of the lines at length, for they are the most instructive, and the rest at a brisk march — partly because the conclusion matters, and partly because it is a model of how to argue a causal claim about the inside of a neural network, which is a skill this course means to teach you by example.

*The first line* you have: **co-occurrence**. The heads form, and the capability arrives, in the same window, in model after model. Suggestive, no more — but suggestive in model after model of the family.

*The second line* is my favourite, and it is the one I particularly invite you to admire: **co-perturbation**. If the formation of induction heads *causes* the onset of in-context learning, then anything that *moves* the one should drag the other along with it. So the researchers reached into the architecture and moved it. Recall why a one-layer model cannot form induction heads: the pivotal fact — “I was preceded by Honoria” — must be computed by one attention step before another can use it, and one layer has only the single step. The researchers then introduced a small architectural cheat, a modification the field calls a *smeared key*: each position’s key is blended with a fraction of the *previous* position’s key, so that every key arrives with a whiff of its predecessor already mixed in. The annotation the previous-token head exists to write is now supplied, gratis, by the architecture itself — and a *one-layer* model, which could never form an induction head honestly, can suddenly implement prefix-matching with its single step. The prediction writes itself: if the hypothesis is right, smeared one-layer models should *acquire* the in-context learning transition that ordinary one-layer models entirely lack, and in deeper models the cheat should let the machinery form *earlier*, dragging the capability’s onset earlier with it. Both predictions held. The phase change moved about like furniture, and the capability moved with it, everywhere, in lockstep. When you can shift an effect at will by perturbing its hypothesised cause, sir, you are no longer in the suggestion business.

*The third line* is the surgical one: **ablation**. Take a small trained model, reach in, and *disable* precisely the induction heads — switch off those components and no others — and measure what happens to in-context learning. It degrades, substantially. Knock out the mechanism and the capacity it is hypothesised to carry falls away with it. This is the interventional logic we shall study as a formal discipline in our sixth episode, here in its plainest form.

*The fourth line*: in small models, the mechanism is not a black box but a *traced circuit* — the very clockwork of Part One. The claim “these heads perform pattern completion” rests not on correlation but on an explicit, verified algorithm. One is not arguing that an unknown something does the job; one knows what the something is and how.

*The fifth line* anticipates a later part of this episode: induction heads, examined closely in larger models, turn out to perform not only literal copying but a spectrum of *more abstract* pattern-completions — matching on similarity rather than identity, completing structural analogies, even carrying patterns across languages. The mechanism, that is, has visible *range* — enough range to plausibly underwrite a general capability rather than a parlour trick.

*And the sixth line* is the honest extrapolation: in *large* models — where the full circuitry is too tangled to trace and too redundant to cleanly ablate — the same outward signatures persist: the same phase change, at the same developmental moment, with induction heads measurably forming across it. The causal proof lives in the small models; the large ones exhibit every symptom consistent with the same diagnosis. The researchers were scrupulous about the gradient of confidence — demonstration in the small, strong inference in the large — and I shall be equally scrupulous on their behalf.

So: it is *not* established that induction heads are the *whole* of in-context learning — that would be too neat, and later work has indeed found further layers to the story, with more sophisticated pattern-matching machinery sharing the load in large models. The responsible statement, and the one the six lines support, is this: a substantial and causally-demonstrated *portion* of in-context learning is carried by induction heads and their relatives; the induction head is the *foundational* instance — the simplest member of a family of context-exploiting circuits, the one whose birth marks the capability’s onset and whose removal degrades it. When you next watch a model apparently *learn* a task from three examples in its prompt, I would have you picture, underneath the apparent magic, a great parliament of prefix-matchers reaching back through the context, finding the places where the present pattern occurred before, and copying forward what followed. Much of the magic is *that*, generalised and multiplied. Jeeves does not oversell; neither does he undersell, and this finding deserves its full weight.

### Part Five — Phase Changes at Large: Grokking, and the Question of Emergence

I said the induction bump has relatives, and the most celebrated of them deserves its place in this episode, both because it is a marvellous story and because together the two findings reframe one of the noisiest debates in the field — the debate over *emergence*.

The story is called **grokking**, and I shall tell it here only far enough to set it beside the bump, because the tenth episode owns it in full — the clock opened gear by gear, the reasons it waits so long, and the theory of simplicity underneath. The short form: a small transformer, set the almost insulting task of modular addition, memorised its training examples quickly and then sat at *chance* on the unseen ones for an interminable stretch — long past the point any reasonable person would have stopped the run — before test performance abruptly leapt from chance to essentially perfect. Crammed first, understood later, on a timescale no undergraduate could get away with. The mechanistic interpreters took the trained model apart and found it had not learned addition the way a schoolchild does: it had reinvented the problem as *rotation around circles*, composing angles and reading off where the combined rotation landed — trigonometry, discovered unprompted by gradient descent. And the instruments they built from that mechanism — **progress measures**, gauges reading how far the circular circuitry had *formed*, as distinct from how well the model scored — told the story the test accuracy had concealed: the general algorithm had been assembling *gradually*, beneath the memorised crust, for the whole of the silent period, and the final thunderclap was merely the model cleaning house, discarding the now-redundant lookup table. Continuous construction within; discontinuous behaviour without.

Now set grokking beside the induction bump and you have the makings of a sane position on *emergence* — a topic on which a great deal of ink has been spilled, much of it warm. One camp points to capabilities that appear abruptly as models scale or train, and speaks of unpredictable leaps. Another camp retorts, with some justice, that many reported leaps are artefacts of the measuring stick — that a harsh pass-or-fail metric will register a cliff where the underlying competence climbed a gentle ramp. The mechanistic findings let one say something more precise than either slogan. Yes: underlying structure tends to form *gradually*, and gauges built from the mechanism show smooth progress where behavioural metrics show nothing — the mirage camp has a point. And yes: the *behavioural* consequences of that formation can nonetheless be genuinely, consequentially abrupt — a circuit that is ninety per cent assembled confers nothing; assembled, it confers everything; the bump in the loss curve is not an artefact of anyone’s metric. Both things are true, at different levels of description, and the appearance of contradiction was only ever the result of watching a construction site exclusively from the street. The practical moral for anyone charged with forecasting what the next model will do — and forecasting is, increasingly, a safety discipline — is that behaviour is a lagging indicator. If you wish to see capabilities coming, you must learn to read the progress of the machinery, not merely the score on the test. That is an argument for this entire field, made by two small models that learned, respectively, to copy and to count.

### Part Six — Beyond Literal Copying: Soft Induction and Task Vectors

I have, so far, described the induction head doing something quite literal: it finds an exact repeat of the current token and copies the exact token that followed. Stated so baldly, it sounds like a parlour trick of limited use — and if that were all it did, it would not underwrite in-context learning, because the tasks we set models in their prompts are rarely a matter of copying verbatim repeats. So let me show you how the same machinery, loosened, reaches a great deal further than literal repetition. This generalisation is the fifth of our six lines of evidence, given its proper due — and it is what carries induction from a curiosity to a workhorse.

The first loosening is *fuzziness*. Nothing in the mechanism requires the match to be exact. The prefix-matching step is, recall, a comparison of a query against keys in the geometry of the residual stream — and that geometry, as the first episode insisted, encodes *meaning* as direction, not merely token identity. So an induction head can match on *similarity* rather than identity: it can attend back not only to the literal previous occurrence of the current token, but to occurrences of *similar* tokens, or tokens playing a *similar role*. Researchers have found heads that do exactly this — *soft* or *semantic* induction heads, which complete patterns over paraphrases and near-repeats, not just over verbatim ones. The clerk no longer needs the page to be word-for-word identical; a page *about the same thing* will do. And the family’s range runs further than paraphrase: among the specimens documented in large models are heads performing what can only be called *translation induction* — completing a pattern laid down in one language when it recurs in another, matching “the same thing said before” across the boundary of the language it was said in. The pattern being matched, evidently, lives at the level of meaning, where the first episode taught us the directions are.

The second loosening is *abstraction of the pattern itself*. Consider a prompt that establishes not a repeated token but a repeated *structure* — say, a list in which each line gives a country and then its capital, several times over, and then gives a country and stops, expecting the capital. There is no literal repeat here; “France” never appeared before. But there is a *positional and relational regularity* — “the slot after a country-name, in this list, is filled by a capital” — and induction-like machinery, attending to the *structure* of the preceding lines, can carry that regularity forward and fill the slot. This is the bridge from copying to genuine few-shot learning: the model treats your worked examples as a pattern to be continued, and continues it. *That* is how three examples in a prompt teach a fourth: the model induces the regularity that the examples instantiate and applies it to the new case.

And now I come to a finding I particularly want you to carry forward, because it links this episode to our final one and because it is, on its own, rather beautiful. When a model is given a few-shot prompt — several worked examples of some task — researchers have discovered that the model often *compresses the task itself into a compact internal representation*, a single direction-laden vector sitting in the residual stream at a particular position, which encodes *what the task is*. The field calls these **task vectors** or **function vectors**. The remarkable demonstrations are two, and they are mirror images. First, you can *extract* this vector — read it out of the model as it processes a few-shot prompt — and find that it stands for the task in a portable way. Second, and more striking, you can *inject* it: take that extracted vector, drop it into the model on a *completely different* prompt that contains *no examples at all*, and the model will *perform the task anyway*, as though it had been shown the examples. Hand it the function vector distilled from twenty antonym pairs, give it the bare word “hot” with no examples in sight, and out comes “cold” — the lesson administered, as it were, by injection rather than instruction. The examples have been distilled into a thing you can carry from one context to another and *install*. The finding has been replicated across model families, and the vectors even *compose*: certain pairs of task vectors, added together, yield the combined task.

Hold that, sir. We have just seen, in passing, the seed of the entire technique that our seventh episode is built around — the practice of *steering* a model by adding a chosen vector into its residual stream to change what it does. Here it arrives organically: the model, learning a task from examples, manufactures exactly the sort of object that we will later learn to manufacture ourselves and use as a control lever. The thing we will do deliberately to *steer* the model is something the model already does to *teach itself*. I shall say no more now; I merely plant the flag.

### Part Seven — What Is the Learning in In-Context Learning?

Before the engineering, a question with more philosophy in it than this series usually permits itself, though I shall keep the philosophy on a short lead. We have established that induction machinery carries much of in-context learning. But what *is* in-context learning, at bottom? When a model improves at a task from examples in its prompt, what kind of process is occurring? The field entertains three answers, they are not as compatible as they first appear, and the dispute among them is one of the liveliest in the science — so you should know the positions, sir, if only to nod at the correct moments.

The first answer is the one this episode has been building: **retrieval**. In-context learning is prefix-match-and-copy, generalised — the model improves with context because it can find where the present situation occurred before and reuse what worked. On this view, nothing resembling *learning* happens at inference; there is only an increasingly sophisticated lookup, softened by semantics, abstracted over structure. The induction family is the mechanism, and the magic is a parliament of librarians.

The second answer is more startling, and it arrived from a deliberately stripped-down experiment. Researchers trained transformers, from scratch, not on language but on bare mathematics: prompts consisting of input–output pairs from some function — points from a random straight line, say — followed by a fresh input wanting its output. Nothing to retrieve here in any ordinary sense; every prompt presents a *new* function, never seen in training, and the model must estimate it from the in-context points alone. And the trained models do it — for linear functions they match, almost exactly, the predictions of the *optimal* classical estimator, the least-squares fit a statistician would compute; and they extend the feat to sparse functions and even small decision trees, in each case approximating the appropriate textbook algorithm. The model behaves, in other words, not like a librarian but like a *statistician*: it appears to be running an estimation procedure, inside the forward pass, on data supplied at inference time.

And the theorists promptly made the startling part respectable. It was shown, by explicit construction, that an attention layer of a particularly simple kind can implement *one step of gradient descent* on a regression problem laid out in its context — the queries, keys, and values arranged so that the layer’s output is precisely the prediction after a single optimisation step, with further layers supplying further steps. The architecture, that is, can contain a small working model of its own manufacture — a watch with a tiny watchmaker inside — and trained toy models were found, in the simplest linear settings, to have converged to configurations approximating this — though how far the correspondence survives in full softmax transformers on realistic data remains genuinely contested. On this second view, in-context learning is *learning* in the full technical sense: an optimisation procedure, executed in activations rather than weights, fitting the data in the prompt.

The third answer splits the difference with Bayesian decorum: the model neither retrieves nor fits, but *infers* — it treats the prompt’s examples as evidence about *which task*, from the great distribution of tasks met in training, it currently inhabits, and conditions accordingly. Recognition, rather than learning — the examples do not teach the model the task so much as remind it which of its existing competences is wanted. The task vectors of the last part sit very comfortably in this picture: a compact internal answer to the question “what is being asked of me?”, distilled from the evidence and then acted upon.

Where does the truth lie? The honest answer — and the one the evidence currently supports — is that the question “which one?” is probably malformed.
